Sharemax & Nova

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The rescue team of the failed multi-billion rand investment scheme Sharemax pulls off the most lucrative corporate capture the country has seen to date.

Unique Selling Point:
In 2011 Carte Blanche reported on the property syndication scheme Sharemax that had run into severe trouble after promised returns stopped being paid out to investors. 
Now we report on a devastating twist in the saga — the rescue scheme put in place to refund wronged investors, is turning out to be a self-enrichment scheme in itself – benefitting only a handful of multi-millionaire directors at the expense of 33,000 destitute investors. 


Summary:
Mostly elderly people had invested R5,6-billion worth of their life savings in Sharemax, having been promised massive returns. 

Sharemax published glossy prospectuses on properties all around the country, promising a rate of return far higher than banks — some people got as much as 16% and 19% return on their investments. Investors lived on the monthly pay-outs.

Then the South African Reserve Bank halted Sharemax saying they had contravened the Banks Act, by acting like a bank when taking deposits from investors. It was the biggest-ever collapse of a property syndication scheme in South Africa. Carte Blanche reported that there would be a rescue plan to help investors get back some money.


Further information:
Subsequently a new company was created called NOVA which became the vehicle to house all 66 properties in the Sharemax portfolio while working out how to refund investors. For three years the financial publication Moneyweb tried to gain access to the shareholding of NOVA to assess how the 33,000 investors had been treated.

Nova fought Moneyweb in court, until they were ordered last week to release their shareholding to Moneyweb. Moneyweb has now revealed the degree to which the exploitation of investors had developed that financial journalist Deon Basson first exposed in 2003. That investigation, opposed by Sharemax, cost Basson his life. He died after a massive heart attack from the strain of trying to help uncover the truth of Sharemax as a ponzi scheme.

The directors of Nova, once portrayed as white knights, appear to have pulled off one of South Africa’s greatest-ever corporate captures. The four directors seized absolute control of the company, worth R1.2 billion, for the princely sum of R40 and kept it from public view since 2011, possibly in contravention of the shareholding disclosure provision in the Companies Act.

In 2013 a pensioner committed suicide by shooting himself in the heart outside the offices of Sharemax, illustrating the human toll this story has had.

10’
The rescue plan devised to help thousands of Sharemax investors is struggling to pay back the money ... who's to blame?



15’
What’s happened to the R5-billion invested by over 40,000 people who believed Sharemax's promises of high returns?
DEBBIE GIRONI: They’re using it without our consent…we can’t even vote.



15’
Frustration remains five years into the rescue plan instituted to ensure that Sharemax pay back investors who gave millions to the property syndication group
DEBBIE GIRONI: I’d like to see the rescue plan. I’d like to see if we can get our money back, because the money that they’re using is our money.

Script:


In 2010, former teacher Debbie Gironi decided to invest the money she had saved while teaching abroad into South Africa’s largest property syndication group, Sharemax Investments.
UPS SHAREMAX PROMOTIONAL VIDEO: “Sharemax Investments, pioneering the property investment business”
Sharemax offered people the chance to invest in shopping centres owned by the group and to earn a handsome return.
DEBBIE GIRONI, SHAREMAX INVESTOR: I first heard about Sharemax from my dad -- he had a few Sharemax investments which seemed to be doing quite nicely. I don’t remember there being a lot of risks. That’s where I could kick myself.
Debbie did not know that the Reserve Bank had been looking into Sharemax since 2006. She’d just invested over a million rand of her kids’ education funds in Sharemax when, in 2010, the authorities slammed on the brakes. The Reserve Bank said Sharemax contravened the Banks Act by illegally collecting deposits from Joe Public. Debbie’s dad Ken Stevenson had also invested his retirement money.
KEN STEVENSON, SHAREMAX INVESTOR: My belief in retrospect if that they were certainly aware of pending problems coming through for their activities. But it was never ever disclosed to us.
Payouts dried up and investors -- many of them pensioners -- faced losing their money. To avoid a liquidation, a rescue plan was devised in 2012 which saw Sharemax become the Nova Property Group. Nova would continue to run the former Sharemax properties in an attempt to make enough money to repay investors.
LINK: Nova, operating as a rescue plan, gave itself ten years within which to pay back investors – and we’re now in year five.
Despite the interventions, questions remain.
DEBBIE GIRONI, SHAREMAX INVESTOR: I remember Nova was made up of the original Sharemax directors. They were going to act in an administrative function to look after the properties owned by Sharemax. I thought that sounded like quite a good idea at the time and I’m not too sure how everything went wrong.
Nova’s job was to fix the devastation left in Sharemax’s wake. Between 1998 and 2010, Sharemax collected R5,6-billion from about 40-thousand people. Initially their smaller shopping centres did well and people got returns, but financial journalist Julius Cobbett says it was too good to be true.
JULIUS COBBETT, JOURNALIST: They didn’t say this is what you might get, they said this is what you will get and it was about 12% at the time which was a good return.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Why didn’t you buy the spin?
JULIUS COBBETT, JOURNALIST: An immediate red flag was the commissions they were paying people selling the product, which was round about 10% -- why do you have to pay a broker so much commission to sell your product if it’s good.
Heady with the success of good returns from established shopping centres, Sharemax made plans to develop its own malls for billions of rand -- the Zambesi Mall in Pretoria North and The Villa in the city’s Eastern suburbs. Debbie and Ken say there was a mad rush for money in the final days of Sharemax.
DEBBIE GIRONI, SHAREMAX INVESTOR: I had to sign documents over e-mail, you know, within a day. The money had to be deposited the next day.
KEN STEVENSON, SHAREMAX INVESTOR: We were very pressurised ... I can remember one day on a Wednesday turning the bank upside down to get the money through so that I could beat the deadline.
But there was a fly in the ointment for Sharemax: The media, and in particular award-winning forensic financial journalist Deon Basson. Back in the early 2000s, Basson had started warning that Sharemax was a sophisticated pyramid or ponzi scheme where money from new investments was used to pay out returns to earlier investors. His wife Celia heard him speak to many concerned investors.
CELIA BASSON, DEON BASSON’S WIDOW: And also some people who ... people that asked him that say: “Oh thank you that you warned me not to do it, because I realise now or I’m not going to take the risk anymore.”
JULIUS COBBETT, JOURNALIST: Deon Basson wrote letters to Trevor Manuel and Mandisi Mpahlwa, the Trade and Industry Minister at the time. I think it’s fair to say it’s a ponzi scheme and it is something that the FAIS ombud Noluntu Bam has, has alleged as well.
Sharemax denied that it was a ponzi scheme and in 2006, the company sued Basson for R20-million for defamation. Two years and a million rand in legal fees later, Basson died of a heart attack only days before defending his work in court.
CELIA BASSON, DEON BASSON’S WIDOW: When he had to go to court and he had to start getting an advocate and pay for people, then he realised that they were playing games with him, because every time they tried to postpone it...I think that was quite stressful.
Basson wrote a manuscript titled ‘Public Interest Warriors’ in which he dealt with Sharemax. After his death, Sharemax bought the manuscript from his deceased estate for R600 000. As a result, Basson’s book has not seen the light of day. Forensic auditor Andre Prakke studied Sharemax’s business and would have testified for Basson had the trial gone ahead.
ANDRE PRAKKE, FORENSIC AUDITOR: I think it would have put to rest all the doubts and on-going who’s right and who’s wrong...also it should bring facts to light which is not in the public domain, which was ultimately never disclosed and still not disclosed.
Dominique Haese, who was financial director of Sharemax and became CEO of Nova, still says Sharemax did nothing wrong.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: It was extremely traumatising, 2010, to many many people -- never-mind the investors out there.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Was Sharemax a Ponzi scheme?
DOMINIQUE HAESE: Not ever. It’s not even possible.
Corporate lawyer Connie Myburgh drafted the rescue plan and then became chairman of Nova. He defends the decision to keep two of the old Sharemax directors on.
CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: Those two directors needed to be retained in order to bring the intellectual property and knowledge across.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We’re still here. Everybody else ran away. Nobody cared. Our mission is to grow …
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Why didn’t you run away?
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: Because there was nothing wrong.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Do you now in 2017 disagree with what the Reserve Bank had to say?
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: They did what they had to do, I suppose. A great injustice was done here.
Under the rescue plan, investors had a choice. More than thirty thousand opted to accept debentures under which Nova would try to pay them back within a decade as it generated profit. Only two thousand chose to become shareholders in Nova in the hopes of sharing in any future growth.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: And how’s it going?
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: Under the difficulties obviously with coming out of where the Group has come from and all the negativity, reputational risk that comes with it, funding has come extremely slow over the years.
LINK: It’s with shopping centres like this that NOVA hopes to earn back the money it owes investors.
In 5 years, Nova has managed to pay out R167-million to some 1400 people whose investments were linked to shopping centres that did well -- a drop in the ocean of the R4.36-billion it must repay.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: What’s your income per month in terms of the NOVA group?
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: Five or six million per month.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: It’s not a lot hey…
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: It’s very tough.
Moneyweb editor Ryk van Niekerk and others question the director’s slice of this meagre income pie.
RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: It seems like these four directors are running it as their own business and they have the power to pay themselves these huge salaries, and they do.
ANDRE PRAKKE, FORENSIC AUDITOR: While the rental income is reducing... according to Nova’s financial statements it is R100 million a year, from all these properties and they have got to service all these expenses and if you look at what the internal expenses is, a substantial portion of that money is going to director’s fees. It is the biggest, single line item.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: As a rescue scheme, the allegation is that this has become a self-enrichment scheme for directors.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: If you look at the financial statement historically there is R51 million paid...if you work that out over five years by four people, you’re looking at R2.5 million per person per year.
Around half of Nova’s money is tied up in the two Pretoria malls that were to be the jewels in Sharemax’s crown. Zambesi Mall never attracted a full house of tenants and eventually they all left. Today, it operates as a China Mall and just breaks even. The massive Villa development stands deserted while Nova insists it will find the R1-billion needed to finish it.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We’ve been busy five years and we are very far down the line with two alternatives of external funding coming in to help us finish The Villa.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: If it’s a great shopping centre and if it’s going to make people money, then I wouldn’t care about reputational risk. I would be in there.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: That’s what we say.
CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: That’s what we say, you might not care.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We don’t understand it.
CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: You might not care but the banks care.
Nova says it has already grown the group’s value by a billion rand.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Is Nova rescuing anything?
RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: It seems like they are trying to improve some of the buildings and then to increase their rental income from those buildings. But the problem now is that they don’t have any funding. We need the best possible corporate governance for this company. It’s a rescue scheme.
But Haese says it’s tough for the group to adhere to the so-called King codes of good governance that require, among other things, an independent audit committee on the board.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We adhere to all the Acts, the laws, the Companies Act and all the things that you’re required to adhere to, barring King II being extremely difficult to adhere to on all levels. Nobody’s interested to serve on this board.
DEVI: Reputational risk again?
DOMINIQUE HAESE: Everybody is lambasted in the press. Now, you have to seek somebody that’s completely disconnected in terms of King. It’s very difficult.
It was journalists including Cobbett, then writing for Moneyweb, who took up Deon Basson’s baton.
JULIUS COBBETT, JOURNALIST: It started when I attended a Nova AGM and it was interesting to me that the investors there were not asked to vote on resolutions. The Chairman Connie Myburgh said we already have enough votes to pass all the resolutions. Why does this guy have all the votes, he must own the whole company, him and his mates.
Van Niekerk says Moneyweb wanted to find out who really called the shots at Nova but the company pushed back when asked for details of their shareholders.
RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: When they denied it or refused it quite aggressively, we went to court to get a judgment so that they should reveal it. And 3 years later we got it.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: 3 years later?
RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: They managed to stall this for 3 years.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We were extremely busy far down the line with funding and every time something gets written it hampers that process. So by keeping Moneyweb in court and away without being able to publish anything, it helped the process of achieving funding lines. This is why we’ve been fighting them all along.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Dominique, do you know what you just said?
CONNIE MYBURGH (interrupting): Just listen to what you just said…
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: What?
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: You just said … you just said, and you said it … you said it suited you to keep Moneyweb in court so that they wouldn’t publish articles and because every time they publish an article, it had a negative impact on you getting funding. That’s what you just said.
DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: But it’s correct.
The fight with Moneyweb revealed that the four Nova directors hold 87% of the shares. The 4% of shares held by investors, have no voting rights attached.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Now you got free shares?
CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: I don’t think it’s free … those shares …
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: How much did you pay for it?
CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: We didn’t pay for it, because …
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: You got it for free.
CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: Ja. But those shares only realise value once the debentures have been repaid.
DEVI: But you got free shares.
Nova says debenture holders and shareholders can contact its call centre any time for information. But those waiting for answers tell a different story.
DEBBIE GIRONI, SHAREMAX INVESTOR: I’ve given up on trying to contact the directors of Nova. I’d like to see the rescue plan. I’d like to see if we can get our money back, because the money that they’re using is our money. They’re using it as they wish without our consent. We can’t even vote.

Dominique Haese, who was financial director of Sharemax and became CEO of Nova, still says Sharemax did nothing wrong. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: It was extremely traumatising, 2010, to many many people -- never-mind the investors out there. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Was Sharemax a Ponzi scheme? DOMINIQUE HAESE: Not ever. It’s not even possible. Corporate lawyer Connie Myburgh drafted the rescue plan and then became chairman of Nova. He defends the decision to keep two of the old Sharemax directors on. CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: Those two directors needed to be retained in order to bring the intellectual property and knowledge across. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We’re still here. Everybody else ran away. Nobody cared. Our mission is to grow … DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Why didn’t you run away? DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: Because there was nothing wrong. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Do you now in 2017 disagree with what the Reserve Bank had to say? DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: They did what they had to do, I suppose. A great injustice was done here. Under the rescue plan, investors had a choice. More than thirty thousand opted to accept debentures under which Nova would try to pay them back within a decade as it generated profit. Only two thousand chose to become shareholders in Nova in the hopes of sharing in any future growth. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: And how’s it going? DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: Under the difficulties obviously with coming out of where the Group has come from and all the negativity, reputational risk that comes with it, funding has come extremely slow over the years. LINK: It’s with shopping centres like this that NOVA hopes to earn back the money it owes investors. In 5 years, Nova has managed to pay out R167-million to some 1400 people whose investments were linked to shopping centres that did well -- a drop in the ocean of the R4.36-billion it must repay. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: What’s your income per month in terms of the NOVA group? DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: Five or six million per month. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: It’s not a lot hey… DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: It’s very tough. Moneyweb editor Ryk van Niekerk and others question the director’s slice of this meagre income pie. RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: It seems like these four directors are running it as their own business and they have the power to pay themselves these huge salaries, and they do. ANDRE PRAKKE, FORENSIC AUDITOR: While the rental income is reducing... according to Nova’s financial statements it is R100 million a year, from all these properties and they have got to service all these expenses and if you look at what the internal expenses is, a substantial portion of that money is going to director’s fees. It is the biggest, single line item. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: As a rescue scheme, the allegation is that this has become a self-enrichment scheme for directors. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: If you look at the financial statement historically there is R51 million paid...if you work that out over five years by four people, you’re looking at R2.5 million per person per year. Around half of Nova’s money is tied up in the two Pretoria malls that were to be the jewels in Sharemax’s crown. Zambesi Mall never attracted a full house of tenants and eventually they all left. Today, it operates as a China Mall and just breaks even. The massive Villa development stands deserted while Nova insists it will find the R1-billion needed to finish it. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We’ve been busy five years and we are very far down the line with two alternatives of external funding coming in to help us finish The Villa. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: If it’s a great shopping centre and if it’s going to make people money, then I wouldn’t care about reputational risk. I would be in there. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: That’s what we say. CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: That’s what we say, you might not care. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We don’t understand it. CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: You might not care but the banks care. Nova says it has already grown the group’s value by a billion rand. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Is Nova rescuing anything? RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: It seems like they are trying to improve some of the buildings and then to increase their rental income from those buildings. But the problem now is that they don’t have any funding. We need the best possible corporate governance for this company. It’s a rescue scheme. But Haese says it’s tough for the group to adhere to the so-called King codes of good governance that require, among other things, an independent audit committee on the board. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We adhere to all the Acts, the laws, the Companies Act and all the things that you’re required to adhere to, barring King II being extremely difficult to adhere to on all levels. Nobody’s interested to serve on this board. DEVI: Reputational risk again? DOMINIQUE HAESE: Everybody is lambasted in the press. Now, you have to seek somebody that’s completely disconnected in terms of King. It’s very difficult. It was journalists including Cobbett, then writing for Moneyweb, who took up Deon Basson’s baton. JULIUS COBBETT, JOURNALIST: It started when I attended a Nova AGM and it was interesting to me that the investors there were not asked to vote on resolutions. The Chairman Connie Myburgh said we already have enough votes to pass all the resolutions. Why does this guy have all the votes, he must own the whole company, him and his mates. Van Niekerk says Moneyweb wanted to find out who really called the shots at Nova but the company pushed back when asked for details of their shareholders. RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: When they denied it or refused it quite aggressively, we went to court to get a judgment so that they should reveal it. And 3 years later we got it. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: 3 years later? RYK VAN NIEKERK, MONEYWEB EDITOR: They managed to stall this for 3 years. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: We were extremely busy far down the line with funding and every time something gets written it hampers that process. So by keeping Moneyweb in court and away without being able to publish anything, it helped the process of achieving funding lines. This is why we’ve been fighting them all along. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Dominique, do you know what you just said? CONNIE MYBURGH (interrupting): Just listen to what you just said… DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: What? DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: You just said … you just said, and you said it … you said it suited you to keep Moneyweb in court so that they wouldn’t publish articles and because every time they publish an article, it had a negative impact on you getting funding. That’s what you just said. DOMINIQUE HAESE, NOVA CEO: But it’s correct. The fight with Moneyweb revealed that the four Nova directors hold 87% of the shares. The 4% of shares held by investors, have no voting rights attached. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Now you got free shares? CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: I don’t think it’s free … those shares … DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: How much did you pay for it? CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: We didn’t pay for it, because … DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: You got it for free. CONNIE MYBURGH, NOVA CHAIRMAN: Ja. But those shares only realise value once the debentures have been repaid. DEVI: But you got free shares. Nova says debenture holders and shareholders can contact its call centre any time for information. But those waiting for answers tell a different story. DEBBIE GIRONI, SHAREMAX INVESTOR: I’ve given up on trying to contact the directors of Nova. I’d like to see the rescue plan. I’d like to see if we can get our money back, because the money that they’re using is our money. They’re using it as they wish without our consent. We can’t even vote. ENDS

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The rescue team of the failed multi-billion rand investment scheme Sharemax pulls off the most lucrative corporate capture the country has seen to date.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In 2011 Carte Blanche reported on the property syndication scheme Sharemax that had run into severe trouble after promised returns stopped being paid out to investors. Now we report on a devastating twist in the saga — the rescue scheme put in place to refund wronged investors, is turning out to be a self-enrichment scheme in itself – benefitting only a handful of multi-millionaire directors at the expense of 33,000 destitute investors.
metadata.Summary: Mostly elderly people had invested R5,6-billion worth of their life savings in Sharemax, having been promised massive returns. Sharemax published glossy prospectuses on properties all around the country, promising a rate of return far higher than banks — some people got as much as 16% and 19% return on their investments. Investors lived on the monthly pay-outs. Then the South African Reserve Bank halted Sharemax saying they had contravened the Banks Act, by acting like a bank when taking deposits from investors. It was the biggest-ever collapse of a property syndication scheme in South Africa. Carte Blanche reported that there would be a rescue plan to help investors get back some money.
metadata.Further information: Subsequently a new company was created called NOVA which became the vehicle to house all 66 properties in the Sharemax portfolio while working out how to refund investors. For three years the financial publication Moneyweb tried to gain access to the shareholding of NOVA to assess how the 33,000 investors had been treated. Nova fought Moneyweb in court, until they were ordered last week to release their shareholding to Moneyweb. Moneyweb has now revealed the degree to which the exploitation of investors had developed that financial journalist Deon Basson first exposed in 2003. That investigation, opposed by Sharemax, cost Basson his life. He died after a massive heart attack from the strain of trying to help uncover the truth of Sharemax as a ponzi scheme. The directors of Nova, once portrayed as white knights, appear to have pulled off one of South Africa’s greatest-ever corporate captures. The four directors seized absolute control of the company, worth R1.2 billion, for the princely sum of R40 and kept it from public view since 2011, possibly in contravention of the shareholding disclosure provision in the Companies Act. In 2013 a pensioner committed suicide by shooting himself in the heart outside the offices of Sharemax, illustrating the human toll this story has had.
